annotation_description: Playing Breeding Pool on turn 1 when there's nothing to cast this turn. If it enters tapped, a Forest would have accomplished the same thing while preserving the Breeding Pool for a later turn when paying 2 life to have it enter untapped would actually matter (e.g., needing UG on a critical turn). If it enters untapped, 2 life is wasted for no benefit.

Gem3P Sarge chose not to play a land on Turn 1's postcombat main phase despite having Blooming Marsh and Gloomlake Verge in hand. Since it's Turn 1 (three or fewer lands), Blooming Marsh would enter untapped. Missing a land drop is almost never correct, especially when the land enters untapped and enables future plays like the Impending cost of Overlord of the Balemurk ({1}{B}) on Turn 2.

Playing Forest instead of the second Breeding Pool on turn 2 wastes the opportunity to play Breeding Pool untapped for free (≤2 other lands check). On a later turn with 3+ lands, the Breeding Pool will either enter tapped or cost 2 life. The hand has two Forests, so one could be played later without issue.

Earthbending the Breeding Pool turns it into a 1/1 creature (0/0 with a +1/+1 counter), making it vulnerable to removal. The opponent has black mana available and could easily have cheap removal like Requiting Hex (which destroys creatures with mana value 2 or less - lands animated this way have mana value 0). If the Breeding Pool dies as a creature, it returns tapped, costing a tempo turn. More importantly, the Forest is a basic land that's more expendable - losing a Forest to removal is far less costly than losing a dual land. The Breeding Pool provides both green and blue mana, which is critical for casting Wistfulness with UU spent. Earthbending the Forest would have been the safer and more strategically sound choice.

Gem3P Sarge has 8 cards in hand and only 1 land on the battlefield. They chose not to play a land on turn 3, missing a critical land drop. They have Blooming Marsh (which would enter untapped since they control ≤2 other lands), Gloomlake Verge, and Starting Town available to play. Missing this land drop means they'll have to discard to hand size (going from 8 to 7), losing a card for free. Additionally, they're falling behind on mana development against an opponent who already has 2 lands and a mana creature (Badgermole Cub). With expensive cards like Overlord of the Balemurk, Wistfulness, and Superior Spider-Man in hand, they desperately need to hit land drops.

The player cast Requiting Hex to kill Badgermole Cub before playing a land. They have Blooming Marsh, Gloomlake Verge, and Starting Town in hand and only one land (Starting Town) on the battlefield. By playing a land first (Blooming Marsh, which enters untapped with ≤2 other lands), they would have access to both {B} and {C}/{any color}, giving them the option to cast both Requiting Hex AND Overlord of the Balemurk's Impending cost ({1}{B}) in the same turn. Casting Requiting Hex first using Starting Town's {C} tap means they can still play a land, but Starting Town is now tapped, so they'd need to use the new land for Overlord's Impending — Blooming Marsh provides {B} but they'd need {1}{B} total, which requires two lands untapped. By playing Blooming Marsh first, then tapping both lands, they could cast Requiting Hex ({B} from Blooming Marsh) and still have... wait, that still taps both lands. Let me reconsider: with 1 Starting Town on board, they need {B} for Requiting Hex. Starting Town produces {C} or pays 1 life for any color. If they play Blooming Marsh first (enters untapped), they have 2 lands. They can tap Blooming Marsh for {B} to cast Requiting Hex, then tap Starting Town for... they only have {C} or pay life for colored. For Overlord Impending {1}{B}, they need 2 mana including {B}. After casting Requiting Hex they'd have only 1 untapped land remaining. So they can't cast both regardless with only 2 lands. The sequencing of land-before-spell is still technically correct practice (play land first to maximize options), but in this case it doesn't change the available plays materially. Killing Badgermole Cub is reasonable to stop ramp, though deploying Overlord Impending (a must-answer threat that also mills and recurs Wistfulness from graveyard) could be argued as higher priority since the Cub is already tapped.

annotation_description: The player chose to cast Overlord of the Balemurk (for its impending cost of {1}{B}) over Requiting Hex targeting the opponent's Badgermole Cub. The Badgermole Cub is a significant threat because it adds extra green mana whenever a creature is tapped for mana, accelerating the opponent's ramp strategy. Killing it immediately with Requiting Hex (which costs only {B} and can legally target the 2-mana-value Cub) would slow down the opponent's development. Meanwhile, Overlord cast for impending won't be a creature for 5 turns and only mills/recurs on entry — it doesn't impact the board right now. The better sequencing would be to kill the Cub first (the immediate threat enabling ramp), then deploy Overlord next turn. Additionally, the player could play a land (Gloomlake Verge or Starting Town) this turn to have more mana available, cast Requiting Hex for {B}, and still have mana for Overlord's impending cost next turn.

annotation_description: On turn 4 with only 2 lands in play (Starting Town and Blooming Marsh), casting Overlord of the Balemurk for its impending cost of {1}{B} is a reasonable tempo play. However, the player had Requiting Hex available to destroy the opponent's Badgermole Cub (a 2/2, mana value 2), which is generating extra mana for the opponent via its 'whenever you tap a creature for mana, add an additional {G}' ability. The Badgermole Cub also likely earthbent a land into a creature. Killing it with Requiting Hex for just {B} would have been more impactful this turn, as the opponent's mana acceleration from the Cub is a significant threat - it enables earlier Craterhoof Behemoth or other big plays. The player could have played Gloomlake Verge as their land drop, then cast Requiting Hex to kill the Cub, and still had mana for Overlord's impending cost next turn. Instead, by casting Overlord first, they missed the opportunity to remove the mana-doubling creature while it was tapped and vulnerable. That said, the Overlord impending is also a strong play, so this is a minor sequencing issue rather than a major blunder.

Played Multiversal Passage (which costs 2 life to enter untapped) when Willowrush Verge was available and would enter untapped for free while producing the same green mana needed (since Timmy already controls Forests and Islands). This wastes 2 life for no meaningful advantage.

Opponent has no creatures on the battlefield, so all attackers would deal damage unblocked. Timmy has at least 2 Badgermole Cubs and Spider Manifestation for 6 free damage against a 17-life opponent. Not attacking throws away significant free damage with no downside.

Discarding Wistfulness when a second copy of legendary Superior Spider-Man is in hand. Wistfulness can be evoked for just {G/U}{G/U} making it castable even when mana-starved, while holding two copies of a legendary creature means one will likely be stranded. There's already a Wistfulness in the graveyard for Superior Spider-Man to potentially copy.
